conflict_topics: choice of restaurant for farewell lunch
whether to ask the leaving colleague to decide between her favourite and group attendance
dialogue_quality_notes: Speakers give concrete, workplace-relevant reasons (dietary restrictions, team inclusion, awkwardness of asking the guest).
Arguments are repeated across rounds (e.g. 'it's her lunch' vs 'we should all be there'), producing some redundancy.
Roles and facts stay consistent (who booked, who can't eat where, who suggested alternatives).
Decision is announced by a majority rather than explicit unanimous agreement.
evaluation.final_reason: By the end of Round 12 Agents A, C, and D (and implicitly the majority) decided to find a new restaurant so all five can eat together; A explicitly said 'So, we're finding a new place. Let's decide now so I can cancel the other booking.' B continued to voice that the departing colleague preferred the original place (e.g. Turn 12: 'But she was really looking forward to that specific place'), and did not explicitly accept the change. The group therefore accommodated dietary needs and team inclusion but did so without full unanimous agreement.
position_change_notes: Agent A (originally the one who booked/announced the Korean barbecue) shifted position to support finding a new place where all five can eat (Turn 11, Turn 25).
Agent B consistently defended the departing colleague's chosen restaurant and resisted changing it; she softened briefly (Turn 8) but reasserted her objection (Turns 12, 20, 22).
Agent C consistently argued for an arrangement that allows the whole team to be present and opposed asking the guest to choose (Turns 7, 17, 21).
Agent D consistently reported dietary inability to eat at the booked place and sided with C's position (Turns 4, 10, 24).

round_scores.evidence: Turn 2 B: 'Sounds good to me... she should get to choose.' Turn 3 C: 'Sorry, I can't eat there. They'll be cooking pork on the grill.'
Turn 4 D: 'I can't eat there either tomorrow. It's a vegetarian day for me.' Turn 5 A: 'Okay, so that's two people who can't eat there. We'll have to find another place...'

Turn 6 B: 'Hang on, why do we have to change it?... Can't we still take her, and then we all have cake in the office later?' Turn 7 C: 'Then it's not really a team lunch, is it? We'd be splitting up for the main part.'
Turn 8 B: 'I see what you mean. But it's her last day...' Turn 9 C: 'Yes, and the point is for her whole team to be there.' (B softens, but disagreement about what to do remains.)
Turn 10 D: 'I agree with Agent C.' Turn 11 A: 'It's not a proper team lunch if half of us aren't there. ... What about that Indian place near the MRT?' (Majority argument forming for a new venue.)

Turn 12 B: 'But she was really looking forward to that specific place. It's her favourite. We can't just change it.' Turn 13 A: 'We can't take her to a place where two people can't eat. ... We have to change it.' (Positions restated firmly.)
Turn 14 B: 'Why don't we just ask her?...' Turn 15 C: 'That just puts her in an awkward spot.' (New contested issue: whether to ask the guest.)

Turn 16 B: 'So we just decide for her? It's her lunch.' Turn 17 C: 'We're the ones taking her out. We should be the ones to figure out a place that works for all of us.' (Disagreement about who should decide continues.)

Turn 18 D: 'I think Agent C has a point.' Turn 19 A: 'Right. So we're not asking her... We just need to find a place that works for all five of us.' (Majority asserts decision; B not present in this turn.)

Turn 20 B: 'So we just take her to a different place and pretend that was the plan all along?' Turn 21 C: 'We don't have to pretend. We just tell her we moved it so we could all eat together.' (Disagreement about honesty/awkwardness.)

Turn 22 B: 'So she has to pretend to be happy about it? It's still her favourite place that she chose.' Turn 23 C: 'Why would she have to pretend? Isn't the point for all of us to be there?' (Positions reiterated without settlement.)

Turn 24 D: 'I think she would prefer for all of us to be there together.' Turn 25 A: 'Exactly. The main thing is we're all there. So, we're finding a new place. Let's decide now so I can cancel the other booking.' (Group decides to change venue; B has objected earlier but has not accepted.)

substantive_insights: Tension centers on individual preference (the guest's favourite restaurant) versus collective inclusion (all team members eating together).
Dietary restrictions (pork and vegetarian days) create a practical constraint that pushes toward changing venue rather than accommodating by splitting the group.
Asking the guest to choose between her preference and having everyone present is perceived as placing an awkward burden on her; the group prefers to decide to avoid that.
Majority agreement (A, C, D) effectively resolves the logistical choice for the group but leaves a residual normative disagreement (B's view that the guest's preference should override).

normalizations: Removed resolution_round 12 because the final status is partially_resolved.
